svg.title: Global negative feedback loop in the ST-70
svg.desc: The full signal path from input to speaker, with a single resistor sampling the OPT 16Ω secondary and returning it to the input stage cathode. The feedback opposes any change the amp introduced, dramatically reducing distortion and output impedance.
svg.text: Global negative feedback — one wire, big consequences
A single resistor from the 16Ω OPT tap back to the input stage cathode wraps the whole amplifier in a feedback loop.

g.data-tooltip: Audio input. Comes from the source (preamp, phono, etc.) via the input jack.

SUMMING JUNCTION — physically the input stage's cathode resistor network.
The input signal and the feedback signal meet here. The feedback is wired to OPPOSE the input (180° out of phase), so the input stage actually sees:
effective_input = audio_in − (small fraction of) output_at_speaker
If the output starts to distort (deviate from a clean copy of input), the feedback signal becomes a slightly distorted version of input. Subtracting that from input cancels some of the distortion. The more loop gain, the more cancellation.

INPUT STAGE — the first voltage amplifier.
In the ST-70 this is the pentode section of the 6GH8A driver tube. Modest gain (~50×), low noise.
The cathode of this stage is where the negative feedback signal arrives — it modifies the effective ground reference of the input tube, opposing any change at the output.

PHASE SPLITTER — produces the two opposite-phase signals push-pull needs.
In the ST-70 this is the triode section of the 6GH8A, configured as a cathodyne (split-load) phase splitter. See the phase-splitting page for the topology.

PUSH-PULL OUTPUT STAGE — two EL34s in class-AB push-pull.
Big gain, big power. Also the biggest source of distortion in the amp (output tubes are non-linear under load). The feedback loop dramatically cleans up this stage's distortion.

A-470 OUTPUT TRANSFORMER — couples the high-voltage / high-impedance tube plates to the low-impedance speaker.
The transformer's frequency response and phase shift become PART of the feedback loop. Anything that delays the signal here delays the feedback too — which can cause oscillation at frequency extremes if the loop isn't designed carefully. The A-470's extraordinary bandwidth (−1 dB from 6 Hz to 30 kHz) is what makes the ST-70's modest feedback amount stable.

SPEAKER OUTPUT.
The output across the secondary is what gets sampled and fed back. The feedback resistor connects to the 16 Ω tap specifically — higher impedance taps give a stronger feedback signal for the same speaker output.

FEEDBACK RESISTOR — typically ~6-10 kΩ in the ST-70.
This value sets the AMOUNT of feedback. Larger resistor → less feedback (more 'natural' amp character, more distortion, higher output impedance). Smaller resistor → more feedback (more correction, more risk of instability if the loop isn't well-designed).
The ST-70's feedback is modest by audiophile standards — about 13-16 dB. Some designs use 20+ dB, some use zero. There are religious arguments about the right amount.

g.text: ① Lower distortion — by a factor of (1 + loop_gain).
At 16 dB feedback (~6× loop gain), distortion drops ~6×.
② Lower output impedance — better speaker damping.
Helps the amp grip the speaker cone, tighter bass.
③ Wider, flatter bandwidth — feedback fights roll-off.
Without it the A-470 alone would roll off earlier.
① Stability — too much feedback + a slow OPT can
cause oscillation at high frequencies. Compensation needed.
that some listeners actually like. Audiophile-tier debate.
③ Tighter design constraints — the OPT and entire
loop must be carefully phase-matched to stay stable.
